prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

After Cai Guo-Qiang Quick, before the sun rises, get up one more time, my grandmother. The artist won’t mind if you borrow his sky ladder. Place your foot on the bottom rung and keep climbing, even though you’re a skeleton with a broken neck from falling downstairs on Guy Fawkes night. The ladder is wrapped in gunpowder, and he’s lit the touchpaper. Your bones are ascending firecrackers. You’re half a kilometer high now, halfway to the universe, my joy-gardener. I hope you find a garden with rich black soil for your black roses, hybrids like you— half white half Indian, half woman half flower, their roots twined through your skull, you who were transplanted among the pale roses of a British family. Your skin now a mix of photons and soot. What do you find up there? Is there a hothouse? Are there alien hands with deft brushes pollinating stars? Remember how your tomatoes kept yielding more planets? Are there constellations of exotic fruit now you’ve reached the top? Have you gone back enough in space-time to when you were alive? The ladder is charred, the hot air balloon that held it up is about to collapse. The explosions are over. Cai showers his head with champagne, as his 100-year-old granny watches on her cell phone.Did you see it? He asks,did you hear the whoosh, the rat-tat-tat at the starry door? You can go back to sleep now

outputs.L1:
**After Cai Guo-Qiang**

Quick, before the sun rises, get up one more time, my grandmother. The artist won’t mind if you borrow his sky ladder. Place your foot on the bottom rung and keep climbing, even though you’re a skeleton with a broken neck from falling downstairs on Guy Fawkes Night.

The ladder is wrapped in gunpowder, and he has lit the touchpaper. Your bones are ascending firecrackers. You’re half a kilometer high now, halfway to the universe, my joy-gardener. I hope you find a garden with rich, black soil for your black roses—hybrids like you: half white, half Indian; half woman, half flower—their roots entwined through your skull. You, who were transplanted among the pale roses of a British family. Your skin now a mixture of photons and soot.

What do you find up there? Is there a hothouse? Are there alien hands with deft brushes, pollinating stars? Remember how your tomatoes kept yielding more planets? Are there constellations of exotic fruit now that you’ve reached the top? Have you gone back far enough in space-time to when you were alive?

The ladder is charred. The hot-air balloon that held it aloft is about to collapse. The explosions are over. Cai showers his head with champagne as his 100-year-old granny watches on her cell phone.

“Did you see it?” he asks. “Did you hear the whoosh, the rat-tat-tat at the starry door?”

You can go back to sleep now.
outputs.L2:
**In the Wake of Cai Guo-Qiang**

Hurry, Grandmother—rise once more before dawn. Surely the artist will let you use his ladder into the heavens. Step onto its lowest bar and climb, despite being only bones now, your neck snapped in that fall down the stairs on Guy Fawkes Night.

Gunpowder coils around the ladder, and the fuse is already burning. As you rise, your skeleton crackles like a chain of fireworks. Soon you are five hundred metres above the earth, midway to the cosmos, my cultivator of happiness.

May there be a garden waiting for you, its dark, fertile earth ready for black roses. Let them be crossbreeds in your image: partly white, partly Indian; partly blossom, partly woman. May their roots thread themselves through your skull—you who were replanted among the washed-out blooms of a British household. Now your body is made from light particles mingled with ash.

What is waiting at that height? A greenhouse, perhaps? Unknown beings wielding delicate paintbrushes to fertilize the stars? Your tomato plants once produced world after world; now that you have arrived at the summit, do strange fruits form whole constellations around you? Have you travelled so far backward through space and time that you have returned to the years when you lived?

The ladder has burned black. The balloon supporting it is close to giving way. The detonations have fallen silent.

Cai pours champagne over his hair while his century-old grandmother looks on through her mobile phone.

*Did you watch it?* he asks. *Did you catch the rushing sound, the burst of rat-a-tat against the entrance to the stars?*

Now you may sleep again.
outputs.L3:
The speaker imagines their deceased grandmother ascending Cai Guo-Qiang’s gunpowder-lit *Sky Ladder*, climbing its fiery rungs toward the farthest reaches of the universe. During this ascent, her damaged body undergoes a luminous transformation: her broken skeleton becomes a string of firecrackers, while her skin dissolves into mingled light and soot. Death is thus reimagined not simply as disappearance, but as a spectacular release of energy into the cosmos.

Gardening imagery further commemorates the grandmother as a “joy-gardener” who nurtures hybrid black roses. These flowers reflect both her mixed Indian and white heritage and her experience of being transplanted into a British family. The metaphor presents her as someone who created beauty and belonging despite displacement, cultivating joy in circumstances that may not always have allowed her to feel fully rooted.

As the grandmother climbs, the speaker wonders what she might discover beyond the sky: celestial gardens, unfamiliar fruit, alien creatures carrying pollen, or perhaps a hidden route through space-time that could lead her back to life. Yet the vision remains tenderly aware of its own impermanence. When the fiery ladder finally burns out, Cai celebrates the spectacle alongside his own elderly grandmother. In response, the speaker gently releases theirs from the imagined journey, telling her that she can return to sleep.
outputs.L4:
I can’t reconstruct an existing work from a summary, but here is an original lyrical piece based on those ideas:

When I watch Cai Guo-Qiang’s *Sky Ladder* climb into the darkness, I imagine it was made for my grandmother.

The ladder rises in fire, rung after rung, as though someone has unrolled a burning path between earth and the stars. For a few moments, the night is no longer empty. It has an entrance. It has a direction. It opens above us like a gate.

My grandmother has been dead for years, but in my mind she stands at the foot of that ladder, waiting. She carries nothing. She has already left behind the photographs, the recipes, the clipped stems rooting in glasses of water. She has left behind the questions people asked about where she came from, and the answers that never seemed large enough to hold her. Her life had been divided into colors, countries, names, and silences. Even belonging was something she had to cultivate patiently, like a garden in reluctant soil.

I want the ladder to lead her somewhere those divisions no longer matter.

At its summit, I imagine a cosmic garden: black earth threaded with constellations, fruit trees flowering in every season, vines curling around the moon. There are beds of rosemary and mint, lilies opening their pale mouths, tomatoes still warm from an impossible sun. Every plant she ever tended is there, restored. Nothing wilts. Nothing is uprooted. No hand asks a flower to explain the mixture of its colors.

She begins to climb.

With each rung, the fire illuminates some small piece of her life: her hands pressing soil around a seedling; her face turning toward a kitchen window; her laughter, sudden and bright; the weariness she hid from us. Memory does not return in order. It flashes, disappears, and flashes again. For an instant she is young. Then old. Then every age at once.

The ladder burns upward, but it cannot last. That is part of its beauty and part of its cruelty. Fire consumes the road it creates. The glowing rungs tremble against the sky, and I know that soon they will fail. I want to call out to her—to hurry, to keep climbing—but perhaps she has already reached the place I imagined. Perhaps she does not need to arrive anywhere. Perhaps the ascent itself is enough: one radiant interval in which death loosens its hold and the distance between us becomes briefly passable.

Then the ladder collapses.

The night closes over it. Sparks fall like seeds, fading before they touch the ground. My grandmother is gone again, but her absence feels altered. I no longer picture her wandering between worlds, unable to claim either one. For those few burning moments, she had a path. She was connected to earth by light and to the heavens by longing. She belonged to both.

I let the garden remain above me, invisible but alive. I imagine her kneeling among the stars, her hands dark with celestial soil. I imagine her finally beyond every category that constrained her, tending a place where all roots intertwine.

The smoke thins. The sky returns to darkness. I return to my body, to the room, to the quiet weight of grief.

And because the ladder rose, however briefly, I can let it fall.

She can rest.

So can I.

After the rain stopped, Cai and Guo walked quietly through the old city. The wet streets reflected the lanterns, and the evening air smelled of tea and earth. Cai spoke about leaving to pursue a new life, while Guo listened in silence.

At the bridge, they paused and watched the river flow beneath them. Guo finally smiled and said, “No matter where you go, this place will remain part of you.”

Years after that evening, Cai would remember those words whenever home felt far away.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an experimental elegy for a deceased mixed-race grandmother, inspired by Cai Guo-Qiang’s “Sky Ladder,” blending grief, gardening imagery, fireworks, and cosmic ascent.
counterfactuals.output:
**SKY LADDER FOR GRANDMOTHER, WITH SEEDS**

At dawn we carry your ashes  
past the tomatoes splitting their red mouths,  
past marigolds keeping their small orange vigil,  
past the fence where jasmine has mistaken  
every boundary for a reason to climb.

You were two rivers  
refusing the map’s instruction—  
brown hand, pale hand,  
braided at the wrist of history.  
In your kitchen, nations softened:  
rice steamed beside rosemary,  
chilies flared in the old blue pot,  
and every hunger was called *child*.

Now the garden wears your absence  
like rain that never arrives.

We plant what remains of you  
under the pear tree.

          Bone-salt.  
          Star-flour.  
          A dark amendment to the soil.

Someone strikes a match.

Across the field, gunpowder wakes—  
first a hiss, then a golden rung  
nailed briefly into morning.  
Another. Another.  
A ladder of fire leans against the sky,  
impossible and therefore yours.

You begin to climb.

Not with feet—  
those tender engines have finished—  
but by petal, by spark,  
by the names we called you  
lifting from our mouths:

Grandma. Abuela. Nana.  
The private name your mother gave you.  
The name the census misspelled.  
The name love pronounced correctly.

Each explosion opens  
a chrysanthemum no hand can cut.

Black branches of smoke  
flower over us.  
The heavens, startled, make room.

Below, your garden continues  
its green argument with death:  
beans winding upward,  
worms translating sorrow into soil,  
sunflowers turning their many dark faces  
toward the wound of light.

We thought ascent meant leaving.

But ash falls back—  
softly, everywhere—  
on our hair, the leaves,  
the wet shoulders of stones.

You return as weather.  
You enter the roots.

And high above the ladder’s last burning rung,  
where blue becomes black  
and black fills with ancestral lamps,  
you pause—

half of every country,  
whole as the moon—

then step into the unbordered dark,  
carrying your little tin of seeds.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a lyrical prose poem in which the speaker imagines their grandmother climbing Cai Guo-Qiang’s gunpowder ladder before dawn. Mention her fatal fall on Guy Fawkes night, her black roses and tomatoes, and the artist’s own centenarian grandmother watching by phone.
counterfactuals.output:
Before dawn, I imagine my grandmother placing one slippered foot upon Cai Guo-Qiang’s ladder of fire, climbing the rungs as they flare into being—gunpowder stitching earth to heaven, a bright, impossible seam.

Below, the garden keeps her black roses and tomatoes: velvet mouths, dark fruit, leaves silvered by the hour before birdsong. She climbs past the roof, past the chimney, past the November night in which she fell and did not rise—Guy Fawkes fire still cracking in the distance, every star a small explosion no one could stop.

Higher, Grandmother. Take the burning handrail. Do not look down.

Somewhere, the artist’s own centenarian grandmother watches by phone, her face lit by the little screen as the ladder ascends—one old woman witnessing the dream of another, though mine has already crossed beyond signal, beyond bone.

The fuse runs upward. The sky opens rung by rung.

For a moment, death is not a fall but a climbing: her hands smelling of tomato vines, her dress brushed with the soot of black roses, her body growing lighter with each incandescent step. Then the ladder gutters, dawn gathers its pale ash, and she is gone again—

not downward,

but into the blue.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: After viewing Cai Guo-Qiang’s *Sky Ladder*, write a surreal ekphrastic poem addressed directly to a dead grandmother. Explore race, transplantation into a white British family, space-time, and the possibility of an afterlife among stars and exotic fruit.
counterfactuals.output:
**Sky Ladder for My Grandmother**

Grandmother, the sky has unrolled a ladder  
and set each rung on fire.

It rises from the black mouth of the earth  
as if grief were a dragon  
learning to stand upright.

Did you see it from wherever you are—  
that bright spine stitched into morning,  
the smoke loosening like your hair?

I was transplanted young,  
a dark root lifted dripping from elsewhere  
and pressed into the chalky garden  
of a white British family.

They watered me with tea,  
with careful vowels,  
with names for weather: drizzle, sleet,  
a summer meaning three pale days.

Still, beneath the table, my blood  
kept another calendar.  
Mango moons ripened in the dark.  
Lychees opened their small white eyes.  
A durian, armoured and fragrant,  
orbited my sleep.

Grandmother, which part of me was yours?  
The face that startled school photographs?  
The skin no winter could translate?  
The stubborn seed under my tongue  
that would not answer to English?

I imagine time as Cai’s burning rope—  
not forward, not back, but upward,  
each explosion a door  
briefly remembering its hinges.

Perhaps death is only distance  
mistaken for an ending.

Perhaps you climb past the last blue rung  
into a country without passports,  
where ancestors picnic on Saturn’s rings  
and spit rambutan stones into space.

Perhaps the stars are fruit  
cut open by invisible knives:  
dragon fruit, guava, persimmon—  
their strange flesh full of suns.

Wait for me there, Grandmother.

I will come carrying both my names,  
my borrowed weather, my buried tropics.  
I will bring the white house that raised me  
folded small as a handkerchief,  
and the vanished house before it  
beating like a second heart.

When the ladder burns away,  
leave one rung glowing.

I have spent my life between gardens,  
learning that a graft can flower,  
that ash can travel upward,  
that even the severed root  
dreams in the grammar of stars.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a single-paragraph hybrid of memoir and prose poetry about grief. Use a burning ladder suspended from a hot-air balloon as the central metaphor, and portray the grandmother’s skeleton rising like fireworks toward a cosmic garden.
counterfactuals.output: When my grandmother died, grief became a burning ladder suspended from a hot-air balloon, each rung blazing beneath my hands while the whole impossible craft drifted over the small fields of my childhood: her kitchen window, the blue cup chipped at the lip, the chair where she shelled peas into a silver bowl and told me that every loss was only a door the body could not fit through. I climbed because there was nowhere else to go, smoke braiding my hair, flame erasing each rung after I left it, and far below, the living gathered like dark seeds around her grave. Then the earth opened—not cruelly, but like a curtain—and my grandmother’s skeleton rose in a bright white rush, every bone a spark, her ribs flowering into chrysanthemums of light, her fingers scattering comets, her skull crowned with brief gold fire. She ascended past the balloon, past the moon’s pale porch, toward a cosmic garden where stars hung like fruit and nebulae unfurled their violet leaves; and though I called after her, she did not turn, or perhaps she turned in the only way the dead can, becoming everywhere at once. The ladder burned on above the world, and I understood that mourning was not the fall but the climbing: the heat, the height, the stubborn reach toward someone already blooming beyond us.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a haunting, intimate response to the documentary *Sky Ladder: The Art of Cai Guo-Qiang*, imagining that the artwork allows the narrator’s grandmother—an Indian-white gardener who died after breaking her neck—to briefly return to the universe before going back to sleep.
counterfactuals.output:
Watching *Sky Ladder*, I thought of my grandmother—the Indian-white gardener whose hands always smelled of crushed stems and wet soil, who could coax green life from anything, until a fall broke her neck and returned her body to the earth she had spent so long tending.

When Cai Guo-Qiang’s ladder ignited, rung by rung, into the dark, it did not seem to rise toward heaven so much as tear heaven open. For a few trembling seconds, fire gave the sky a spine. I imagined my grandmother waking inside that brightness.

Not resurrected exactly. Loosened.

She lifted from the black soil with leaves caught in her hair, her old nightdress carrying the pale glow of gunpowder. The universe recognized her hands. Stars opened like jasmine. Nebulae leaned toward her as seedlings once had. She touched nothing, yet everything grew brighter.

I wanted to ask whether death had hurt. Whether she had been lonely. Whether she remembered us. But the ladder was already burning itself away, each rung becoming smoke the moment it appeared.

So I only watched her climb.

At the top, she turned—not young, not healed, but wholly herself—and for an instant her face held all the colors she had carried: brown earth, white petals, the green shadow under a leaf. Then the sky folded around her.

The last sparks fell like seeds.

My grandmother went back to sleep, and the universe, having briefly remembered her, went dark again.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
